501.quote_or_event: On Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur, according to Sikh tradition, Guru Gobind Singh came out of his tent and asked for five Sikhs willing to offer their heads. The crowd fell silent in fear, but five came forward one after another. They were then revealed alive, and these five, the Panj Pyare, became the first members of the Khalsa.
501.explanation: The Harvard Pluralism Project recounts the tradition of the Guru testing his followers by the fear of death before founding a new order on those who passed.
501.tie_back: The Kural says a person should be trusted with office only after being tested in four ways, the last being fear for one's life; the founding of the Khalsa rests on exactly such a test.
501.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, 'The Khalsa' (paraphrase of Sikh tradition)
501._accuracy_note: A strong fit for the fear-of-death test, which the source presents as Sikh tradition; it covers only one of the Kural's four tests (virtue, wealth, pleasure, fear).

502.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
502.explanation: Guru Nanak tells his hearers to see God's light in everyone and not to ask about anyone's caste or social rank.
502.tie_back: The Kural asks that trust go to someone of good family who fears any stain on his name; Guru Nanak rejects birth and status as a measure of a person, so Sikhism would keep the Kural's sense of shame but not its test of lineage.
502.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
502._accuracy_note: Included as a candid contrast: Gurbani rejects judging people by birth, which conflicts with the Kural's emphasis on good family; it agrees only on valuing character.

503.quote_or_event: “Everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator are infallible.”
503.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that every human being is liable to err and that freedom from error belongs to God and the Guru alone.
503.tie_back: The Kural says that even the learned and seemingly flawless will rarely be found free of some ignorance when closely examined; Guru Nanak says the same of everyone.
503.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 61, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
503._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match on the universality of human fallibility; Guru Nanak's exception for God and the Guru adds a theological point the Kural does not make.

504.quote_or_event: “Good deeds and bad deeds-the record is read out in the Presence of the Lord of Dharma.”
504.explanation: In the closing salok of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak pictures a person's good and bad actions both being read out and weighed before the divine judge.
504.tie_back: The Kural says to look into a person's virtues, then his faults, and judge him by whichever prevails; Japji Sahib likewise has both columns of the record read before judgement.
504.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib (closing salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
504._accuracy_note: Good on weighing good and bad together, but the judgement in Japji Sahib is divine and final, while the Kural describes a ruler assessing a candidate.

505.quote_or_event: “Apply the Touchstone of Truth to your mind, and see if it comes up to its full weight.”
505.explanation: Guru Nanak borrows the goldsmith's touchstone and scale: a person's inner life is to be tested against truth as gold is tested on the stone.
505.tie_back: The Kural calls a person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and meanness; Guru Nanak uses the same touchstone image for testing a person's worth.
505.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 22, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
505._accuracy_note: The touchstone image matches exactly, but Guru Nanak applies it to the mind against truth rather than naming deeds as the test.

506.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them.”
506.explanation: Kabir warns against keeping company with the saakat, the person cut off from God, because such a one has no inner bond to hold him back from wrong.
506.tie_back: The Kural says not to trust those who are cut off from all ties, since without attachments they feel no shame; Kabir likewise warns against relying on those cut off from the bond that restrains.
506.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
506._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Kural's 'cut off' people lack kin and community, while Kabir's saakat is cut off from God; the shared idea of a missing restraining bond is partly interpretive.

507.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool never works out right.”
507.explanation: In a salok in Asa Ki Vaar, Guru Angad says that a bond formed with someone who lacks understanding cannot succeed, however it began.
507.tie_back: The Kural warns that trusting people who lack the needed knowledge, merely out of fondness, brings every kind of folly; Guru Angad says affection for a fool never works out.
507.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
507._accuracy_note: A strong fit on fondness for the ignorant ending badly; Guru Angad speaks of friendship generally rather than of entrusting someone with office.

508.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with the faithless cynics; they would bring you to ruin.”
508.explanation: Kabir warns that close association with those turned away from God ends in ruin for the one who keeps their company.
508.tie_back: The Kural says that putting confidence in someone unexamined brings endless sorrow; Kabir likewise warns that the wrong companion brings ruin.
508.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 93) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
508._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Kabir warns against a known kind of companion rather than against trusting without examination, and says nothing of harm to descendants.

509.quote_or_event: “First, examine the merchandise, and then, make the deal.”
509.explanation: Guru Nanak gives a trader's rule: test what you are dealing in before you commit to it.
509.tie_back: The Kural says to trust no one without examining him and, once he has been examined, to trust him; Guru Nanak's rule puts the testing first and the commitment after.
509.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
509._accuracy_note: Very close in structure (examine first, then commit); the verse speaks of merchandise and, in its context, of spiritual choice, not of persons in office.

510.quote_or_event: “One who has no faith in the True Guru, and who does not love the Word of the Shabad, shall find no peace, even though he may come and go hundreds of times.”
510.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that someone who withholds trust from the Guru gains nothing however often he returns, and remains without peace.
510.tie_back: The Kural says that doubting one who has been tested and trusted brings unending trouble; Gurbani likewise says that withholding faith from the proven Guru leaves one without peace.
510.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 591, Raag Vadhans, Vadhans Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
510._accuracy_note: Partial: both tie lasting trouble to misplaced doubt, but the verse concerns faith in the Guru, not a ruler's trust in a tested servant, and does not address trusting the untested.
